name: Tetrahydrogestrinone (THG / The Clear)

lead: THG, nicknamed The Clear, is an oral steroid made by modifying the gynecological drug gestrinone, taken by athletes for muscle and performance. It surfaced in 2003 when a used syringe was handed to anti-doping officials, and Don Catlin's UCLA laboratory identified it; it became central to the BALCO scandal.

It binds the androgen receptor about as tightly as DHT, also activates progesterone receptors, and binds the glucocorticoid receptor. Rat studies showed it promotes muscle growth. It is known mostly from doping history and detection research rather than from appearance or bodybuilding use.

paras: It was used by athletes as an oral steroid designed to evade existing doping tests; it was never approved for medical use.

It has never been tested in clinical trials, so effects in people are uncharacterised; infertility, acne and hirsutism are listed with prolonged use. It is a US Schedule III substance and banned in sport.

angle.text: A designer steroid made in 2003 to dodge doping tests, taken by athletes for more muscle mass. It is potent in laboratory assays and promoted muscle growth in rats, but has never been studied in people.

lead: Tetrahydrogestrinone (THG), nicknamed "The Clear", is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid made by chemically modifying the gynecological drug gestrinone. It was never approved for medical use and never sold as a product [1][2]. It was designed for one purpose, to build muscle and strength in athletes while escaping the drug tests of the time, which looked only for known substances [1][3].

It became known in 2003 as the first prominent "designer steroid". A spent syringe containing it was passed to the US Anti-Doping Agency, and Don Catlin's UCLA Olympic Analytical Laboratory identified it by mass spectrometry; the findings were published in 2004 [1][4]. The episode was central to the BALCO scandal, which involved sprinters, baseball players and other athletes, and ended in guilty pleas, prison terms and the stripping of Olympic medals [1][5][6].

Laboratory studies show THG binds strongly to the androgen receptor and also to progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors, and it promoted muscle growth in rats [1][2]. No human clinical safety or efficacy trials exist.

In appearance and bodybuilding culture THG is a historical reference rather than a compound in circulation: it is cited as an example of how steroid chemistry can be altered, and as the case that pushed anti-doping laboratories toward screening for unknown steroids [7][8][9].
infobox: Schedule III (scheduled by the FDA in 2005) [1]

paras: THG is an estrane steroid, a 17-alpha-alkylated derivative of nandrolone, closely related to trenbolone, gestrinone, metribolone and norbolethone [1]. Wikipedia describes the design logic as a small change to gestrinone: converting an ethynyl group to an ethyl group turns a norethisterone-type compound with weak androgen-receptor activity into a norethandrolone-type compound with strong activity [1]. A 2004 Science review called it the first true designer androgen, produced in what it characterised as a sophisticated illicit manufacturing setting [3].

The history of THG is largely the history of BALCO, the Bay Area Laboratory Co-operative, founded in 1983 in Burlingame, California, and presented by Victor Conte as a blood-testing and supplement business [5]. Conte's account and USADA's differ on some details, and Wikipedia's Conte biography notes that USADA says he developed THG with the chemist Patrick Arnold [10].

Patrick Arnold (1966-2026), a Connecticut-born organic chemist and amateur bodybuilder known as the father of prohormones, had earlier introduced androstenedione to the North American market in 1996 [11]. According to Arnold's account, summarised on Wikipedia, Conte contacted him in 2000 seeking undetectable drugs; Arnold offered norbolethone, which he had synthesised in 1998, and in 2001, after norbolethone drew scrutiny from testers, he switched to supplying THG [11]. Wikipedia reports that Arnold designed THG using steroids BALCO had marketed, such as norbolethone and desoxymethyltestosterone, along with trenbolone and gestrinone, on the premise that testers were unlikely to detect a novel compound [1]. Arnold has been quoted as saying a couple of drops under the tongue was enough, consistent with reports of its potency [1].

Wikipedia notes that THG, norbolethone and desoxymethyltestosterone were not banned when they were created and were hard to detect, and were distributed to elite athletes in track and field, baseball and football [11].

In June 2003 the sprint coach Trevor Graham anonymously contacted USADA, named Conte as the supplier of an undetectable steroid and supplied a syringe containing traces of the compound [5]. Catlin's laboratory identified the contents, synthesised the compound for comparison and developed a urine screen using liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry; applied to 550 existing athlete samples, the test produced 20 positives, according to Wikipedia's BALCO article [1][4][5].

On September 3, 2003, IRS, FDA, San Mateo narcotics task force and USADA agents searched BALCO's facilities, and Greg Anderson's home was searched two days later; agents reported finding customer lists and containers labelled as steroids and growth hormone [5]. The FDA issued a statement in October 2003 and scheduled THG in 2005 [1].

Athletes named in connection with THG include sprinters Marion Jones and Dwain Chambers and baseball players Barry Bonds and Jason Giambi [1]. Customer records reviewed in the case named athletes in baseball, track and field, boxing, cycling, American football and other sports; Arnold alleged that Bonds and Gary Sheffield received THG, and both denied knowing about it [5].

Marion Jones, who won three gold and two bronze medals at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, had denied doping for years. After Conte said on ABC's 20/20 in December 2004 that he had supplied her, she said her coach Graham gave her THG as a flaxseed oil supplement and that she used it from 1999 to the end of 2002. She pleaded guilty on October 5, 2007 to lying to federal agents, surrendered her medals, and received a six-month prison sentence in January 2008 [6]. Conte described the history of the sport as one of corruption and cover-up in that 2004 interview [10].

On July 15, 2005, Conte and Anderson pleaded guilty to illegal steroid distribution and money laundering; Conte served four months in federal prison and Anderson 13 and a half months [5][10]. Arnold was sentenced in 2006 to three months in federal prison followed by three months of house arrest [11]. Tammy Thomas and Trevor Graham were later convicted of false statements or obstruction, and Barry Bonds was convicted of obstruction of justice in 2011, a conviction overturned on appeal in 2015 [5]. Reporters Lance Williams and Mark Fainaru-Wada published the book Game of Shadows in 2006 and refused to identify a source for grand jury leaks; the case against them ended in 2007 when an attorney, Troy Ellerman, pleaded guilty to the leak [5].

THG binds the androgen receptor with affinity comparable to dihydrotestosterone and is reported to activate androgen and progesterone receptors more potently than nandrolone or trenbolone, roughly ten times in assays, which Wikipedia attributes to extra van der Waals contacts with the receptor [1][2][12]. Unusually for an anabolic steroid, it also binds the glucocorticoid receptor strongly, which has been linked in the literature to possible weight-loss and immunosuppressive effects [1][2]. It has no estrogenic activity [1]. Studies in rats found it stimulated muscle growth and increased prostate and seminal vesicle weights [2]. A 2006 comparison of crystal structures of the human androgen receptor ligand-binding domain bound to various agonists examined the molecular determinants of binding affinity [12].

In vitro toxicology work has compared THG with trenbolone and testosterone: a 2008 study measured the potency of the three to induce micronuclei in V79 cells [13], and a 2012 study reported dioxin-like effects through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor in cell experiments [14].

THG (13-beta,17-diethyl-17-beta-hydroxygon-4,9,11-trien-3-one) has the formula C21H28O2 and a molar mass of 312.45 g/mol. It is derived from gestrinone by hydrogenating the ethynyl side chain, and resembles trenbolone [1][2][4]. A 2004 paper described its synthesis by hydrogenation of gestrinone and its characterisation by mass spectrometry and NMR spectroscopy [4].

Catlin's team identified THG with mass spectrometry and developed a urine test using liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry [4]. Later reviews argue that THG illustrated the weakness of targeted testing, which looks for known substances and their metabolites, and prompted methods intended to flag unknown anabolic steroids, including screens combining androgen bioassays with accurate-mass spectrometry [7][8][9][15]. A 2012 review described the emergence of designer drugs such as THG as an influence on sports doping testing [15], and a 2013 review described the continuing bioanalytical challenge of detecting unknown steroids [16]. Wikipedia's THG article calls it the second reported designer anabolic steroid [1].

Because it was never clinically tested, its effects in people are not characterised. Wikipedia lists infertility in men and women, acne and hirsutism as expected with prolonged use, and notes that glucocorticoid-receptor binding could bring immunosuppression [1]. A Mayo Clinic Proceedings review discusses cardiovascular toxicities of performance-enhancing substances in sport more generally [17], and general reviews of anabolic steroids list cardiovascular, hepatic and behavioural effects among reported harms of the class [17][18].

THG is a Schedule III anabolic steroid in the United States, where the FDA scheduled it in 2005 [1]. Grokipedia reports that its emergence prompted regulatory reclassification [2]. It is prohibited in sport. The 2005 amendment to the Controlled Substances Act that banned prohormones followed the same period of scrutiny and cost Arnold's prohormone company much of its sales [11].

Coverage of THG is largely coverage of BALCO: the 2004 ABC 20/20 interview with Conte, Williams and Fainaru-Wada's reporting and book, and a White House Correspondents' Association award to the two reporters in April 2005 [5][10]. Conte continued in business, founding the supplement and training company SNAC in 2011, and died in November 2025 [10].

Wikipedia reports that THG was regarded as the drug of choice for invisible record-breaking in athletics [1]. Analytical chemists describe its identification as a turning point that pushed anti-doping laboratories toward screening methods able to flag unknown steroids [7][8][9].

No studies found of THG as a treatment or in controlled human use. Research has consisted of analytical detection work, receptor assays, in vitro toxicology and rodent studies, including a 2005 study reporting muscle accretion in orchidectomized male rats [1][2][4][7][8][13][14]. For context, a 2004 review of anabolic-androgenic steroids in sport notes that studies using supraphysiologic doses of testosterone have shown increases in strength and improvements in body composition [18].

lore.intro: THG is discussed in sport and bodybuilding circles as a cautionary and historical case, and the claims below are those made by the people involved and by commentators rather than by forum communities.

claims.claim: THG was undetectable because testers could not look for a compound they did not know existed.
A tiny amount, a couple of drops under the tongue, is enough.
THG is a superior muscle builder.
Athletes did not know what they were taking.
The whole sport was doing it.

timeline.event: Patrick Arnold introduces androstenedione to the North American market [11].
Conte approaches Arnold seeking undetectable drugs; Marion Jones wins three golds at the Sydney Olympics [11][6].
Arnold switches from norbolethone to supplying THG, by his account [11].
Spent syringe delivered to USADA; THG identified at the UCLA lab [1][4].
Discovery, synthesis and urine detection published; Conte's ABC 20/20 interview in December [4][10].
FDA schedules THG; Conte and Anderson plead guilty on July 15 [1][5].
Arnold sentenced; Game of Shadows published [5][11].
Marion Jones admits lying to federal agents about steroid use and surrenders her medals [6].
Barry Bonds convicted of obstruction of justice; overturned on appeal in 2015 [5].
